name: Japanese Blue
lede: Japanese Blue is a muted, greyish green despite its name, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as first used in 1892, with no documented link to any specific Japanese dye or pigment in the sources we have.

sections.title: A name that misleads the eye
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates this color's first recording to 1892, on plate 30 J 2, but neither that source nor any other in our library explains the connection to Japan [1]. The ISCC-NBS system classifies this hex value as a grayish green, not a blue at all, a mismatch between name and swatch worth noting before trusting the label on sight [1]. In Munsell terms it reads 2.0BG 4.4/2.5, dark and low in chroma [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[dark-porcelain-green]] and [[saul]], at 2.9 and 3.1 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to this color in 269 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.13 percent, and in 119 by the stricter within-painting measure, more common than 62 percent of the named colors we track [2]. Inside those paintings it most often sits as a hidden color, 45 percent of the 119 [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 2.5 times the expected rate, and shows up at 4.5 to 5.5 times the expected rate in Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings specifically [2].

The earliest match in our archive dates to 1300, in a painting attributed to Giotto, with the latest from 1941, 203 dated paintings in all, 630 years before the name's own earliest record, 1930 [1], a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [1][2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
